newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles hold selloff paper in first week of trading.
newsitem.headline: Poles hold selloff paper in first week of trading.

text.p: Poles have been slow this week to change National Investment Fund (NFI) units into fund shares, the first week they can do so, but analysts said this could change as the funds' expected listing next month approaches.
NFI units in the country's mass privatisation programme already trade on the Warsaw Stock Exchange.

"People are thinking very rationally...if you change your NFI unit into shares it's an irreversible order and (currently) you can't sell NFI shares on the bourse, so it's a kind of freezing of assets," said Marcin Billewicz of ING Barings.
Later on Wednesday the Warsaw bourse is expected to clear the shares of the 15 NFIs for public trade and set their debut date for as early as mid-June.
Under the government's NFI scheme, shares in more than 500 mid-sized companies are allocated to the 15 NFIs run by foreign and domestic management firms.

From Monday Poles have had the opportunity to exchange the NFI unit for 15 shares, one in each fund, which have 31,026,185 shares each. On Wednesday the National Securities Depositary (KDPW) said 3,372 units had been converted into shares.

ING Barings' Billewicz said the exchanging of units into shares would likely pick up the week before the funds' listing, as some investors might anticipate low supply at early sessions and therefore seek to take profits after price rises.
Analysts said large investors might otherwise prefer to wait several months for the greater liquidity caused by conversion by smaller players, as the units themselves were currently very liquid.
They said investors might also be waiting for the units' price to rise since the commission for such sales was lower than for share sales.
Jacek Koczwara, an analyst at BGZ brokerage, said large investors seeking to hold sway over a fund might exchange units into shares in the near term.

"Some of the institutions that bought units to gain control over a fund...could exchange units into shares to show that they already are in a fund and another institution that would want to take over that fund could have problems," he said.
